analytic.title: Response-Time Guarantees in ATM Networks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: We present a method f o r providing response-time guarantees in Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) networks. The method is based on traditional real-time CPU Response-Time Analysis (RTA), and is intended to be used f o r admission control of hard real-time trafic. The method determines i f a new connection can be admitted without violating the strict timing requirements specified f o r the new as well as old connections.

We illustrate the merits of our method by comparing it with Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) and the Calculus for Network Delays (CND). Two types of comparisons are made. In the first, we evaluate how well the associated analysis can accommodate different trafic scenarios and loads, and in the second comparison we use simulation to compare observed worst-case behaviors with estimates obtained by the analysis. The comparisons clearly indicate that RTA outperforms both WFQ and CND f o r a set of realistic traffic scenarios.
'in [9] we show that this also holds for RTA

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The use of communication networks in modern realtime systems is rapidly increasing. Many applications using the services of these networks have strict timing requirements. For these applications, statistical guarantees, e.g. in terms of "message loss probability" or "average message delay", are not sufficient. Instead, a firmer commitment is needed from the network, saying that it will al- ways deliver all messages completely and within specified deadlines (with reservation for hardware failure and external physical interference). Several methods for providing such guarantees have been proposed in the literature [6, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 21,281. They all provide or assume some mechanism of bandwidth sharing, and have an associated analysis that can be used by an admission control procedure to d priori answer the crucial question:

div.head: Can the Quality of Service (QoS) requirements of a new connection be met, while not violating the requirements of already admitted connections?
div.p: A positive answer means that the connection can be admitted. A negative answer means that if the new connection is admitted the QoS of the new connection, as well as the QoS of already admitted connections, may be violated.

It is important that solutions to the real-time admission control problem can be easily incorporated with existing network standards. It must also be possible to make efficient implementations, supporting the very high bandwidth of current and future networks. Furthermore, an admission control scheme must allow for high utilization of network resources. Since not all connections may require absolute guarantees it should be possible to integrate hard real-time traffic with other QoS classes which do not require absolute guarantees on the timely delivery of messages. An additional benefit would be if the analysis could be incorporated with an existing framework for real-time systems analysis. This would allow system designers to use the same technique for assessing the timely behavior of the entire system, including both CPU and network scheduling.

In this paper we present an extended version of the Response-Time Analysis (RTA) method introduced in [9]. RTA has been developed for admission control of hard realtime traffic in ATM networks. In [9] we present RTA for single-switch ATM networks with unique priorities for each connection. In this paper we provide a generalization of RTA to handle multiple switch ATM networks and also to allow several connections (streams of messages) to share priority. Furthermore, we present a heuristic algorithm for assigning priorities to streams.

We have focussed on ATM, since it is likely that ATM will be used in industrial control systems and other safety critical applications, simply because it will be the cheapest high bandwidth communication technology available.

In addition to presenting RTA, this paper focusses on evaluating RTA. We use two complementary methods for evaluation. In the first, we evaluate how well the analysis can accommodate different traffic scenarios and loads. In the second method, we use simulation to evaluate the precision of the analysis, by comparing observed worst-case be-haviors with those obtained by analysis. Both evaluations are based on "benchmarking", in that they compare the behavior of different methods in a limited number of realistic scenarios.

RTA is based on a very simple priority queuing mechanism that provides a clear separation between bandwidth and deadline requirements. This gives RTA a potential of offering a bandwidth utilization outperforming currently popular bandwidth reservation schemes, such as Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) [6, 14, 151. We validate this by comparing RTA and WFQ for some realistic traffic scenarios. In addition, we compare RTA with the Calculus for Network Delays (CND) [ 5 ] , which is an alternative analysis method when using priority queuing.

Paper Outline: In Section 2 we give a brief introduction to ATM and the considered methods for providing hard real-time guarantees in ATM networks. Section 3 presents our traffic model. Sections 4 and 5 presents the extended Response-Time Analysis (RTA) method, and our priority assignment algorithm. In Section 6 we introduce the evaluation methods and evaluated scenarios. Section 7 presents the comparative study of call admission controls for RTA, WFQ, and CND, and in Section 8 we present the simulation based comparison. Finally, in Section 9 we discuss our results, draw some conclusions, and indicate possible future work.

div.head: ATM and Real-Time Communication
div.p: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) [ 161 is a high performance, connection oriented, network architecture. Over each connection a stream of fixed size packets, called cells, are transmitted. Each cell is 53 bytes long, consisting of 5 byte header information + 48 byte payload (user data).
Long messages are segmented and sent in consecutive cells in the stream. The ATM network guarantees that cells within a stream is delivered in the same order as they were transmitted.

ATM has been designed to support the high bandwidth, optical signaling, of todays and future information super highways. The streamkell concept have been designed to allow efficient hardware implementations. ATM is proposed as the next generation global telecom network. This network should support a number of communications services, including phone calls, video conferencing and computer communication. ATM is also used for a Local Area Networks (LANs) [ 161.

An ATM network consists of a set of ATM switches. Each switch routes cells from a set of input ports to a set of output ports based on stream identifiers in the cell-headers. At the output port of an ATM switch a port controller multiplexes cells from different streams onto the outgoing line.
The output ports of an ATM switch are governed by a schedulingpolicy, e.g. First In, First Out (FIFO), which de-cides in what order cells are to be dequeued from the output queue.

Scheduling policies can be classified as either workconserving or non work-conserving. A work-conserving policy never let the output link go idle if there are cells queued in the output queue, whereas a non work-conserving policy may let the link go idle even if the output queue is non-empty. An example of a work-conserving policy is FIFO, and an example of a non work-conserving policy is Golestani's "Stop-and430 Queuing" [8].

All work-conserving policies have identical average cell delay, average and maximum buffer need (for any given cell arrival pattern). A non work-conserving policy must by necessity have higher average cell delay, average and maximum buffer need than a work-conserving policy. On the other hand, work-conserving policies tends to increases the burstiness of the traffic, while non work-conserving policies can be used to limit burstiness.

Different applications have different timing and bandwidth requirements. To make sure that each application gets the required Quality of Service (QoS) the network must perform Call Admission (Control (CAC) on new streams. The CAC should ensure that there are enough resources in the network to give the new stream its required QoS, without compromising the QoS of other (already admitted) streams.

There are many methods for performing the CAC. However, most methods only give statistical guarantees, e.g. in terms of "average cell delay". For hard real-time traffic where the QoS must be an absolute guarantee these type of CACs are not applicalble. Instead, a deterministic guarantee, e.g. guaranteeing lhat "the deadline is never missed", is needed. In this paper we only consider methods to provide deterministic QoS guarantees.

To perform the CAC an analysis method is required. Each analysis method is intimately related to a scheduling policy. For some scheduling policies there are many different types of analysis methods, while other scheduling policies have a single analysis method which has been developed together with the scheduling policy.

Our focus in this paper is on work-conserving scheduling policies. Since, as a general rule, work-conserving policies are easier to implement and require simpler buffer management. This makes them more suitable for ATM networks. Work-conserving scheduling policies can roughly be classified as either:

Example of simple policies are FIFO, priority queuing and Earliest Deadline First (EDF). Most of these policies are general purpose scheduling policies, which can be applied to CPU scheduling, network scheduling and scheduling of many other resources. "Simple" policies are conceptually simple and efficient to implement, eventhough most of them are not simple at all to analyze. In fact, it is often very hard, sometimes impossible, to determine the end-to-end responsetimes for messages when simple policies are used. EAample of analysis methods for FIFO and priority queuing are Cruz's Calculus for Network Delays (CND) [5] and our Response-Time Analysis (RTA). For EDF the methods presented in [7] can be applied to ATM networks.
Today, most ATM switches use a simple scheduling policy (e.g. Fore Systems ASX-200BX, ASX-1000 and Cisco LS 1010 all use priority queuing).
In rate based policies each stream is allocated a service rate or a weight. The rate determines how much resources are allocated to the stream.

As a rule, rate based scheduling policies approximate the idealized service discipline Generalized Processor Sharing (GPS). Some example of the class of GPS approximative scheduling policies are: Virtual Clock (VC) [29], Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) [6], Weighted Round Robin (WRR) [18], Slow Start GPS [21] and Multirate PGPS [ 191. Common for all rate based scheduling policies is that the response-time directly depends on the service rate allocated to the stream, and that the service rate corresponds directly to the bandwidth allocation. Thus, to shorten the response-time one must allocate more bandwidth. For streams with tight deadline this may lead to over- allocation of bandwidth, since, in order to shorten the response-time, the stream needs to allocate more bandwidth than it is going to use.

Most rate-based scheduling policies have quite simple analysis methods. However, implementations of these scheduling policies are often very complex. Due to this, rate-based scheduling is currently not a viable solution in ATM networks. However, recent hardware research [22] indicates that it will become possible to produce cost effective rate-based ATM switches. Today, the rate-based WFQ policy is being implemented in Internet routers.

div.head: Traffic Characterization
div.p: Often traffic is characterized in network terminology, using terms such as "average bandwidth", "maximum burst size" and "burst bandwidth". Since such terms mean little (or nothing) for an engineer developing hard real-time applications, we use the following more application oriented parameters, to characterize a stream i: T, is the period (of a periodic traffic source) with which messages are generated. For a sporadic traffic source T, is the minimum message inter-arrival interval. N, denotes the maximum number of cells needed for a message. An ATM cell has 48 bytes of payload, thus, for a stream with maximum message size of X bytes N, = ~4 8 1 .

Ji is the maximumjitter of a periodic traffic source. Many multimedia sources have a significant jitter caused by the processing of image frames in the application or the operating system scheduling on the host where the application executes.

Di is the deadline for end-to-end message delivery, i.e. each message is required to arrive to its destination within Di time units from the time it is generated. This is the hard real-time requirement which always must be met.
We also use the following additional attributes to describe stream i:

hi denotes the number of hops in the path of stream i. hi is given by the routing policy and topology of the network. ti denotes the inter-cell delay when a message passes through a cell spacer (i.e. a traffic shaper, such as a leaky bucket [ 161) at the source node. ti can range from 0 to Ti/Ni, where ti = 0 means that all cells of each message are put into the output queue at once, and ti = Ti/Ni means that the cells are spread out evenly over the whole period.

Ideally, ti should be determined by the network itself. However, since no optimal algorithm to select ti exist, we assume that ti is part of the stream characterization (i.e. it is stated together with the attributes Ti, Ni, etc.). ji denotes the network jitter. The network jitter is caused by network components with variable delay. The network jitter is accumulated along the path through the network. bi denotes the remaining time budget. bi is initialized to Di.
At each network component along the path of stream i the remaining time budget is decreased with the maximum delay at that component.

It is well known that traffic shaping both at the source node and in the network help in reducing congestion and increase utilization of the network'. Thus, shaping through a leaky bucket at the source node is proposed in the ATM standard. Shaping inside the network is usually considered infeasible in ATM networks due to the high bandwidths. Knowing which type of leaky bucket the source node uses, the parameter ti (possibly together with Ti and Ni) can be transformed to leaky bucket parameters.

To characterize the network links we will use the following parameters: c represents the size of an ATM cell, i.e. 424 bits. b denotes the bandwidth of the link in bits per second, 7 is the time it takes to send one cell on the link, 7 = c/b.

In this paper we make the simplification to consider only homogeneous networks, even though heterogeneous networks are straight forward to handle. Thus, we assume that all links have the same bandwidth (b).

div.head: Response-Time Analysis
div.p: In [9] we present RTA for single-switch ATM networks

where each stream has a unique priority. In this paper we generalize RTA to handle multiple switch ATM networks and also allow several streams to have the same priority. RTA has it roots in CPU-scheduling [3,11,131, but has also proven useful to determine response-times for other types of resources, e.g. Controller Area Networks (CAN) [26] and disk drives [23].

The RTA presented in this section assumes that each output queue (in the source nodes and ATM switches) uses priority queuing with "First In, First Out" (FIFO) for cells with equal priority. Thus, the analysis is also applicable to strict FIFO queuing (which can be considered as a priority queue with a single priority level). Figure 1 shows the general structure of the considered network. In the figure, TGi denotes a traffic generating process, which generates messages to be transmitted. These messages are segmented into cells, which are queued in a cell queue associated to TGi. A cell spacer moves cells with a rate of $ from the cell queue to the prioritized output queue. The keason for using a cell spacer is to reduce the burstiness of the traffic and thereby reduce congestion and increase network utilization. From the output queue, cells are sent to the first switch. In the switch, cells are placed in the appropriate output queue, and transmitted further to the next switch until the destination is reached.

It should be noted, that in this paper we focus on the delay in the output queues and in the cell spacer. In [20] we show how to incorporate other delays into the RTA, and also how the maximum buffer need can be calculated.

To understand the different delays involved, it is important to understand the worst-case traffic pattern for a peri-odic stream experiencing jitter. The largest number of cells in a given time interval appears if the first cell, which should arrive in the very beginning of the interval, experience a maximum delay caused by jitter, and if all subsequent cells experience minimum delays.

To calculate the end-to-end delay (the response-time), we first derive the worst-case delay for a message to pass through the cell spacer. 'Then we characterize the worst-case cell arrival pattern to an output queue. From this pattern we derive the worst-case queuing time for a cell. Finally, we describe how the queuing delay changes the shape of the traffic, i.e. we derive the new traffic parameters which can be used to calculate the queuing delay for a subsequent output queue.

div.head: Cell Spacer Delay
div.p: The message delay in a cell spacer can be defined as the time between the message is queued in the cell queue to its last cell is dequeued by the cell spacer. Under the assumption that the jitter, Ji, is zero, the delay before the last cell is dequeued is ti(Ni -1). However, when the jitter is non-zero, the second message may arrive before ti(Ni -1) (i.e. before the first message has passed through the cell spacer). In this case tlhe first message interferes with the second message, and hence the second message will experience a longer delay than ti(Nil) before its last cell is dequeued. If the jitter is large enough it might also be the case that the third message arrives when there are still cells in the cell queue, the same holds for the fourth message, and so forth . . .

When calculating the worst-case delay of a message in the cell spacer we must take this interference into account. First, we note that there is an upper bound on the interference, since we kow that tiNi 5 Ti, and hence, the cell spacer is not over loaded (i.e. its contents will not grow in- definitely). div.p: In order to apply RTA on a subsequent switch it is necessary to capture how the traffic shape (i.e. the traffic parameters) change when passing through the output queue. As already mentioned, traffic passing through a work-conserving queue will increase in burstiness. In our traffic description the network jitter (ji) captures the increased burstiness of a stream.

In general, the added jitter from a network component is equal to the difference between the maximum and the minimum time a cell is delayed in that component. div.head: Priority Assignment and CAC
div.p: There is no known optimal priority assignment scheme for distributed systems. Instead, we propose a heuristic based on Audsley 's locally optimal priority assignment algorithm [2] which we extend with a preordering of streams in deadline monotonic order according to the remaining time-budget (bt).
The combined priority assignment method and CAC, which is executed for each output queue, is described by the pseudo-code in Figure 2 (where nr denotes the number of streams using the output queue).

div.head: Figure 2. Priority assignment algorithm
div.p: This algorithm will assign a unique priority to each stream for each output queue. In this study we assume that the switches have enough priority levels to give each stream a locally unique priority. In the case where streams have to share priorities, the result from our algorithm could be used as an initial ordering from which groups of streams sharing priority are identified.

div.head: Evaluation Methods and Scenarios
div.p: narios used to evaluate the performance of RTA.

In this section we introduce the methods and traffic sce-Two evaluation methods are used to compare RTA with two other Call Admission Control (CAC) methods: the Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) analysis method [14, 151, and Cruz's Calculus for Network Delays (CND) [5]. We have chosen WFQ to represent the rate-base service disciplines since it is the most well known such method. Also, it is the method which closest approximates Generalized Processor Sharing (GPS). CND has been evaluated since it is an alternative method to RTA for priority queuing (PRIQ) and FIFO.
Since CND and RTA are both applicable to PRIQ as well as FIFO we will study both methods on both scheduling policies.

Our first evaluation method investigates how well the considered CACs can accommodate different traffic scenarios and loads. That is, based on randomized traffic scenarios conforming to partiicular traffic profiles, we calculate for different levels of network load the probability of a successful CAC.

Our second evaluation uses simulation to estimate the precision of the analysis methods. By comparing observed worst-case response-times with the worst-case responsetimes calculated by the CACs we obtain a measure of the level of overestimation in the CACs.

div.head: Network Topology
div.p: In all experiments presented here we use a fixed network topology, shown in Figure 3. We define the network load to be the load on the link to the destination node (link 10). We distribute the streams evenly over the 6 source nodes. Thus, when the network load is 100% the load on link 7 will be approximately 33%. VVe have chosen a moderate bandwidth of l0OMbps for each link in the network (i.e. b = lo8).

div.head: Figure 3. Network topology
div.p: Eventhough we only consider a restricted topology, we claim that our results lhave wider applicability. Consider, for instance, a general topology network where the topology in Figure 3 is a sub-network. In such a network there will exist traffic streams which crosses the paths of the streams in the sub-network. This crossing traffic will decrease the performance of the network, but since we are performing a comparative study, and the impact of crossing traffic will be similar regardless of scheduling policy, the results of our evaluations have reasonable validity also for more general topologies.

div.head: Traffic Profiles
div.p: Since the profile of the streams used for comparison will have high impact on the results, we have chosen to investigate three different types of profiles:

1. Random parameters projiles: Each stream will have randomly selected parameters. This will produce streams with a large variation in requirements. The algorithm used to generate the stream parameters has been designed to generate traffic profiles resembling traffic in real-time systems.

div.head: Random stream selection projiles:
div.p: A number of realistic traffic sources and their respective traffic parameters are identified and the scenarios are constructed by selecting a number of such traffic sources. Profiles generated with this method will resemble traffic situations in multimedia networks.

div.head: WFQ-Optimal parameters pro$les:
div.p: Similar to the Random Parameters method, parameters are chosen randomly. However, the deadline is selected to be the lowest possible deadline with which WFQ requires no overallocation of bandwidth. Thus, profiles generated with this method will have an admission probability of 1.0 for WFQ. Obviously, this profile do not correspond to a realworld scenario, but it is interesting to study how other analysis methods compare to WFQ when using WFQoptimal traffic.

From these profile types we have generated the following four traffic profiles: 0 "Control", a random parameter profile, where the average stream corresponds to uncompressed 64kbps connections. This should be similar to traffic in real-time networks dominated by control software messages. 0 "MultimediaKontrol", a random parameter profile, where the average stream corresponds to average quality interactive video connections. This should be similar to traffic in a real-time system with intermixed control and multimedia applications.

0 "Mixed Selection", a random stream selection profile, consisting of a mix of video transfer, audio transfer, and signaling for distributed games and real-time simulations. "WFQ MultimediaYControl", a WFQ-optimal version of the "MultimedidControl" profile above.
A more detailed presentation of the traffic profiles and their parameters are provided in [20].

div.head: Evaluation by Comparing CAC Results
div.p: A good way to understand how well an analysis method performs is to study how much of the network resources it allows to be allocated before the call admission control (CAC) fails. In our comparison the CAC is performed for scenarios consisting of whole sets of streams. The CAC is successful if all streams in the scenario can be guaranteed to meet their respective deadlines.

We will use the admission probability (introduced by Raha, Malcom and Zhao [17]) to measure performance. The admission probability for a specific level of network load is defined as the probability of performing a successful CAC for a scenario with that load. By studying the admission probability for different network loads and different traffic profiles we get a good indication of how well an analysis method performs under different conditions. Naturally, the admission probability is highly dependent on the traffic profile, e.g. in profiles with many tight deadlines, the admission probability can be very low even with light networks load.

We will here only consider the delay in the cell spacer and the network output queues. Other network delays (such as signal propagation) is independent of the scheduling policy, and thus of no interest in this comparative study.
Next we describe how the CAC is performed for the considered analysis methods, and in Section 7.2 we present the evaluation results.

div.head: Results of the CAC comparison
div.p: Indeed, the success of both priority queuing analysis methods in the Mixed Selection is a bit surprising, since WFQ is expected to behave very well in multimedia scenarios. In this study, however, WFQ is performing poorly already at a load of 65%, while priority queuing is successful up until a load of 90'%.
As expected, FIFO queuing does not perform well at all.
In fact, for loads over 15% FIFO queuing can be deemed unusable.

Comparing RTA ancl CND we see that RTA performs better than CND for all profiles and scheduling policies. This is not surprising, since the linear traffic bound in CND's traffic model is ai pessimistic overestimation. In this light, we are actually surprised by the relatively good performance of CND. For 1.he Mixed Selection profile the difference between CND and RTA is negligible. In spite of CND's relative success, we can see that it is probably the case that RTA is strictly better than CND.

An interesting aspect when comparing CND and WFQ is that for the Control and MultimedidControl profiles (figures 5(a) and 5(b)) WFQ is the better of the two on low network loads, while CND outperforms WFQ when network loads increase. The point at which CND starts to perform better than WFQ is dependent on the traffic profile.

For the WFQ MultirnedidControl profile (Figure 5(d)) we see that it is possible to find scenarios where WFQ outperforms all other analysis methods. Thus, we cannot say that RTA is strictly better than WFQ. One must however recall that the WFQ-optirnal scenarios most probably do not correspond well to real-world situations.

div.head: Evaluation by Simulation
div.p: In this section we present simulation results comparing observed response-times with the worst-case bounds obtained by the different analysis methods. The simulations provide an evaluation of how close the worst-cases response-times obtained by analysis are to actual worstcases. sponding Rr values we have high precision in the analysis, in the sense that the analysis captures the actual worst-case well.

The simulations are performed for static traffic scenarios. We use a discrete event simulation model [IO], implemented In the language Erlang [l]. The simulations start from a critical iristarit at each source node, i.e. all streams will initially send as much traffic as possible. Thus, the observed worst-case response-times should be fairly close to the actual worst-case.

The comparison is performed as follows for each scenario generate a set of streams X X is chosen to be sufficiently large to provide a significant load (in our simulations we use a load of 0.9). In X , we randomly select some streams as reference streanis used for comparison. By systematically removing non-reference streams from X , different loads are generated For each load and each analyzed method, a simulation is made to obtain observed worst-case response-times for the reference streams i n X. A measure of the precision of the analysis is then calculated by for each reference stream comparing the response-times obtained by analysis and simulation. Figure 6 presents the result for the profile "Control" The results for other scenarios and profiles we have investigated are similar Comparing the performance of the different analysis methods we see that RTA-PRIQ outperforms the other methods. The precision is lower for FIFO policies than for PRIQ, since the worst-case assumption for FIFO is very pessimistic, and the probability of the worst-case occurring at each switch in the network is practically 0. Both PRIQ methods experience lower precision as the network load increases. The reason for this is that both RTA and CND have higher precision for higher priority streams while low priority streams have relatively high probability to receive better service than the worst-case. When the load increases, more and more streams with higher priority than the reference streams will be added, and hence, the precision decreases.

The precision for WFQ is by far the lowest. The precision for WFQ increases as load increases, contrary to the PRIQ and FIFO policies. However, this is quite natural, since the analysis of WFQ considers each stream in isolation under the assumption that the whole bandwidth of each link is allocated. As the load increases, this assumption becomes more and more valid, thus the precision increases.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have presented and evaluated an extension of the RTA method for Call Admission Control (CAC) in ATM networks. RTA uses traditional real-time response-time analysis [ 3 , 111 to calculate the worst-case response-time of ATM-cells sent through a priority queued ATM-network.

The introduced RTA-extensions allow analysis of multiswitch networks with a limited number of priority levels. This implies that several connections may have to share pri-ority, i.e., priority assignments ranging from a single priority (pure FIFO scheduling) to a unique priority per connection can be handled. Thiis means that many realistic network and traffic situations can be analyzed.

RTA provides a solutions to the real-time admission control problem which can be easily incorporated with existing network standards. In fact, several existing ATM-switches already today provide the required priority queuing. An additional benefit is that the analysis can be incorporated with existing frameworks (e.g. Fixed Priority Scheduling [3]) for real-time system schedulability analysis, thereby allowing system designers to use the same technique for assessing the timing behavior of the entire system, including both CPU and network scheduling (e.g. as proposed in [25]).

In the evaluation we compared RTA with Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ), which makes fixed bandwidth allocations to guarantee both band width and delay requirements, and the Calculus for Network Delays (CND), which uses priorities to control the traffic flow. Priorities allow separate treatment of bandwidth and delay requirements. An additional benefit with priority queuing is its efficient integration of hard real-time traffic with other QoS classes which do not require absolute guarantees. Non hard real-time traffic is simply assigned lower priority, meaning both that it will not interfere with the hard real-time traffic and that it can use any bandwidth not used by the hard real-time traffic. Efficient bandwidth sharing between critical and non-critical traffic is less obvious for rate based reservation schemes, such as WFQ.

In the evaluation, we first compared the admission probabilities of RTA, WFQ, and CND for four traffic profiles, and then we compared the precision of the analysis methods by comparing observed worst-case response-times with calculated worst-case rlzsponse-times.

The resulting comparisons show that RTA has higher admission probabilities and higher precision than both WFQ and CND. In fact, since we have compared RTA with the best methods known to us, the comparison gives evidence that RTA allows higher utilization of network resources than other known methods. Thus, it seems that RTA from this perspective is the best existing method.

We also made the 'observation that WFQ provides the fastest CAC. Performing an RTA CAC is in our experiments up to 100 times slower than performing the corresponding WFQ CAC. The reason for this difference is that the RTA CAC for each connection have to consider the interference from all other connections in the network, while the WFQ CAC can be made independently of other connections.

In conclusion, RTA allows higher utilization of network resources than other mlethods, but the CAC execution time must be improved if P.TA is to be used in larger networks with dynamically arriving connections. Finding a more efficient (probably less exact) CAC, using for instance heuris-tics as proposed in [27], is an important topic for future study.

On the hand, the majority of hard real-time systems (e.g. systems for process control) are quite small and typically have a relatively static set of hard real-time connections. For these type of systems, RTA seems already today the best alternative for providing hard real-time guarantees.
